blocks.text: At the end of the First World War the Ottoman Empire was on the losing side. The Armistice of Mudros, signed on 30 October 1918, was followed within weeks by the occupation of Istanbul by British, French, Italian and Greek forces, and in May 1919 a Greek army landed at Izmir.

The peace treaty that the sultan's government signed at Sèvres on 10 August 1920 would have taken most of the empire apart: Eastern Thrace for Greece, a later vote on the future of the Izmir region, an independent Armenia in the east, French and Italian zones of influence across Anatolia, and the Straits under international control. It was never ratified.

Resistance had already begun in Anatolia. Mustafa Kemal Pasha, an Ottoman general known for the defence of Gallipoli in 1915, landed at Samsun on the Black Sea on 19 May 1919 and rallied the movement at congresses in Erzurum and Sivas. On 23 April 1920 a Grand National Assembly met in Ankara and declared itself the government of the country. It rejected the Treaty of Sèvres.

The War of Independence, *Kurtuluş Savaşı*, was fought on three fronts: against Armenia in the east, against French forces in the south and, above all, against the Greek army in the west. After the battle of the Sakarya in the late summer of 1921 and the offensive of August 1922, Turkish troops entered Izmir on 9 September 1922. On 1 November 1922 the Assembly abolished the Ottoman sultanate.

Peace came with the Treaty of Lausanne, signed on 24 July 1923 between Turkey on one side and Britain, France, Italy, Greece and their allies on the other. It fixed most of the borders of today's Turkey and ended the capitulations, the legal and trade privileges foreign powers had long held in the empire. A separate Greek–Turkish convention, signed at Lausanne on 30 January 1923, made an exchange of populations compulsory and defined it by religion: about 1.2 million Orthodox Christians from Turkey and between 350,000 and 400,000 Muslims from Greece had to leave for the other country. Many had already fled during the wars. The Greeks of Istanbul and the Muslims of Western Thrace were left out of the exchange.

On 13 October 1923 a law made Ankara, then a small town in the middle of Anatolia, the seat of government. On the evening of 29 October the Assembly voted to proclaim the Republic of Turkey, and that night it elected Mustafa Kemal its first president, unanimously. The next day İsmet Pasha, later İnönü, formed the first government. The caliphate, the last office left from the Ottoman state, was abolished on 3 March 1924.

Today 29 October is Republic Day, the biggest of the [national days](a1-u11-culture). The reforms that followed include two you have already met: the [new alphabet of 1928](a1-u01-culture) and the [Surname Law of 1934](a1-u03-culture), which gave Mustafa Kemal the name Atatürk.
Here is the story in the Turkish of this unit, with the past tense:

blocks.tr: Mustafa Kemal 19 Mayıs 1919'da Samsun'a gitti. Sonra Ankara'ya geldi. Savaş 1922'de bitti. 13 Ekim 1923'te Ankara başkent oldu. 29 Ekim 1923'te Türkiye bir cumhuriyet oldu. Meclis Mustafa Kemal'i ilk cumhurbaşkanı seçti.
blocks.en: Mustafa Kemal went to Samsun on 19 May 1919. Then he came to Ankara. The war ended in 1922. On 13 October 1923 Ankara became the capital. On 29 October 1923 Turkey became a republic. The Assembly elected Mustafa Kemal the first president.

questions.q: On what date was the Republic of Turkey proclaimed?
questions.explain: 24 July 1923 is the Treaty of Lausanne, and 23 April 1920 the first meeting of the Assembly in Ankara.

questions.q: Which treaty set most of the borders of today's Turkey?
questions.explain: Sèvres was never ratified; Lausanne replaced it in 1923.

questions.q: In the Turkish text, what does *Savaş 1922'de bitti* mean?
questions.explain: *Bitmek* is to end, and *bitti* its past: it ended.

sources.title: Treaty of Sèvres
sources.note: Signed 10 August 1920; Eastern Thrace to Greece, a plebiscite for Smyrna, an independent Armenia, French and Italian zones, internationalized Straits; never ratified

sources.title: Treaty of Lausanne
sources.note: Signed 24 July 1923 by Turkey, Britain, France, Italy, Japan, Greece, Romania and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes; borders; abolition of the capitulations (article 28)

sources.title: Population exchange between Greece and Turkey
sources.note: Convention signed at Lausanne on 30 January 1923; defined by religion; about 1,221,489 Orthodox Christians and 355,000 to 400,000 Muslims; Istanbul Greeks and Western Thrace Muslims exempted
13 October 1923: law making Ankara the seat of government; 29 October: Republic proclaimed, Mustafa Kemal elected president unanimously by secret ballot; 30 October: İsmet Pasha's first government
